summary: Describes methods for extending the useful life of symmetric keys, since only a limited amount of data can be safely encrypted under one key. It offers two kinds of re-keying based on hash functions and on block ciphers, usable with modes such as CTR, GCM, CBC, CFB, and OMAC. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret code gets easier to crack the more you use it. So you change to a new code every so often, and this explains safe ways to pick the next one.

questions: how to rekey with block ciphers
when should you use external vs internal re-keying
subtitle: Methods to extend the lifetime of symmetric encryption keys.

tldr.problem: Only a limited amount of data can be safely encrypted under a single key before cryptanalysis becomes feasible. Simply renegotiating the key frequently is expensive and disruptive.
tldr.mechanism: Re-keying mechanisms extend key lifetime by periodically deriving new working keys from an initial key. External re-keying happens at the protocol level between messages; internal re-keying happens within a message at fixed data intervals.
tldr.outcome: Protocols can safely encrypt much larger volumes of data under a single master key without expensive renegotiation, improving performance and reducing downtime.

facts.label: Key lifetime limits
facts.value: Set by side-channel and combinatorial attacks

facts.label: ACPKM modes
facts.value: CTR, GCM, CBC, CFB, OMAC with and without master key

today: RFC 8645 is Informational and documents best practices from the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG). These mechanisms are used in standards like TLS 1.3 (which uses serial key updating) and in systems requiring very high data volumes or strong forward secrecy. The document does not define a single mandatory mechanism, but provides the toolkit that standards and implementations can choose from.

sections.title: Key Lifetime Limits and Why They Matter
sections.content:
When you encrypt data under a single key, the more data you encrypt, the more vulnerable it becomes to cryptanalysis. This limit is called the key lifetime. Three kinds of attacks motivate key lifetime restrictions:

First, attacks based on the combinatorial properties of the cipher mode (like birthday collisions) require on the order of 2^(n/2) blocks where n is the block size. Second, side-channel attacks (like timing attacks or power analysis) often do not depend on the mode, and their limits are usually the most restrictive. Third, attacks specific to the cipher's own structure (like differential cryptanalysis) are usually dominated by the other two.

Without re-keying, a protocol must renegotiate the key when it approaches the lifetime limit. Renegotiation is expensive: it terminates data transmission, generates new random material, performs expensive key agreement (possibly including public-key operations), and causes perceptible delays. For high-volume, continuous communications, this is costly.
sections.plainLanguage: Every secret code has an expiration date based on how much stuff you encrypt with it. You can either throw the code away and make a whole new one (which is slow), or use it to make temporary codes that expire faster. The temporary codes are cheaper to make.

sections.title: The Two Approaches: External and Internal Re-keying
sections.content:
This RFC describes two fundamentally different strategies for re-keying. External re-keying operates at the protocol level, independent of the underlying cipher and mode of operation. After processing a certain number of messages, the protocol derives a new working key from the master key. The derived keys are used for data encryption while the master key is used only for key derivation, never for data. External re-keying is protocol-level and mode-agnostic.

Internal re-keying is built into the encryption mode itself. Instead of re-keying between messages, a long message is split into sections. As each section is encrypted, the working key is transformed without leaving the mode of operation. This requires designing new modes (like CTR-ACPKM) and is mode-specific, but it works transparently within standard encryption.

The choice between them depends on the protocol. Protocols with many small messages benefit from external re-keying (which increases the message count). Protocols with long messages benefit from internal re-keying (which increases message size).
sections.plainLanguage: External re-keying is like a factory manager who makes new temporary codes for each batch of work, using the master code only to make those temporary codes. Internal re-keying is like building a code-changing machine directly into the worker's toolbox, so the worker changes codes every hour on the job.

sections.title: External Re-keying Mechanisms
sections.content:
External re-keying derives multiple frame keys (K^1, K^2, ...) from an initial master key K. The master key is used only for derivation; data is encrypted with the frame keys.

Parallel external re-keying generates all frame keys independently from K. This works well for protocols that can process messages out of order or with loss. The simplest form uses a Key Derivation Function (KDF) on a block cipher, encrypting constants (0, 1, 2, ...) under K to produce key material. Alternatively, hash-based KDFs (like HKDF-Expand) can derive keys. For restrictive key lifetime limits, tree-based re-keying builds a tree of key derivations: intermediate keys at each level become input to the next level. This exponentially expands the number of keys reachable from one master key.

Serial external re-keying generates each frame key from a secret state that is updated after each key is generated. This prevents parallel processing but provides forward secrecy: if a frame key K^i is compromised, previous frame keys K^1, ..., K^{i-1} remain secure because they were derived from earlier state values that have been deleted.
sections.plainLanguage: Parallel re-keying is like a key factory that can make all the temporary keys at once from the master code. Serial re-keying is like a key chain where each new key depends on the old key being destroyed—if someone steals key number 5, they cannot go back to steal keys 1 through 4.

sections.title: Internal Re-keying: ACPKM Modes
sections.content:
Internal re-keying transforms the working key during each message, without leaving the cipher mode. The RFC defines ACPKM (Advanced Cryptographic Prolongation of Key Material), a mechanism that re-keys after processing N bits (the section size). Each message starts with a section key; after each N bits, that key is transformed via the cipher itself or a KDF.

ACPKM mechanisms come in two varieties. Without a master key, the initial key is used directly and transformed in place. Modes like CTR-ACPKM and GCM-ACPKM use this. With a master key, a master key derives section keys on demand; modes like CTR-ACPKM-Master, GCM-ACPKM-Master, CBC-ACPKM-Master, CFB-ACPKM-Master, and OMAC-ACPKM-Master use this. Master-key variants allow flexible implementations: the master key can be stored in a Hardware Security Module (HSM) while working keys are generated as needed.

Internal re-keying is transparent to the application: the mode handles re-keying invisibly. It does not affect Initialization Vectors (IVs) or require restarting Message Authentication Codes (MACs). This makes it suitable for long messages or streaming data.
sections.plainLanguage: ACPKM is like a key that automatically refreshes itself every hour of work. The worker does not notice the refresh; they just keep encrypting. You can use the key directly, or store the master key in a vault and have temporary working copies generated on demand.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Mechanism
sections.content:
The RFC provides guidance for protocol designers. For protocols with small, frequent messages (like TLS or SSH records), external re-keying is recommended because it multiplies the number of messages that can be sent before key renegotiation. For protocols with long single messages (like file encryption in CMS), internal re-keying is recommended because it multiplies the message size.

For protocols with loss and out-of-order delivery (like DTLS for encrypted media or ESP in IPsec), external re-keying is preferred because internal re-keying assumes a data stream. However, both can be used together: a protocol can use external re-keying between messages and internal re-keying within each message, combining the benefits of both.

The choice of KDF (block-cipher-based vs. hash-based) affects implementation simplicity and side-channel resistance. Hash-based KDFs (HKDF) separate the key derivation primitive from the cipher, reducing the risk that an attacker can exploit the cipher to break key material. Block-cipher-based KDFs are simpler for implementations that already use a cipher.
sections.plainLanguage: If you send a lot of small messages, re-key between messages. If you send a few huge messages, re-key within each message. You can do both if you want: re-key at every message boundary, then again inside each message.

sections.title: Security Properties and Trade-offs
sections.content:
Re-keying mechanisms extend key lifetime but do not eliminate the need for strong initial keys or sound implementations. The security of both external and internal re-keying assumes that the underlying cipher or KDF is strong.

External parallel re-keying provides forward and backward security for frame keys: compromise of one frame key does not affect others. External serial re-keying provides strong forward secrecy if keys are securely deleted: compromise of the current secret state at time T does not compromise previous secret states at times 1 through T-1.

Internal re-keying mechanisms are transparent but mode-specific. Modes without a master key do not provide backward security (a compromised section key reveals nothing about previous keys only if they are deleted). Modes with a master key allow the master to remain in a secure location (like an HSM) while derived working keys are generated on demand, protecting against key theft.

If an adversary can exploit the encryption interface to mount a chosen-plaintext attack, using the same primitive for both data encryption and key derivation can leak information about future keys. This risk is eliminated by using different primitives (e.g., block cipher for encryption, hash function for key derivation).
sections.plainLanguage: Re-keying adds a layer of protection but does not replace strong codes or careful implementation. If someone steals one temporary key, they should not be able to steal others. If you keep the master key locked in a vault and only use temporary copies, thieves cannot steal it.
